did.abstract: The Wooster Group is a contemporary experimental theater group based at 33 Wooster Street in New York City. Founded by Elizabeth LeCompte and Spalding Gray, the company has been active with an evolving membership since the mid-1970s and has created and performed over 50 works directed mostly by LeCompte. Founding members of the group include Kate Valk, Ron Vawter, Jim Clayburgh, Willem Dafoe, and Peyton Smith.The Wooster Group records features material created, used by, and relating to the Wooster Group's productions, founders, and operations. The bulk of the collection consists of the production files, which includes scripts (many heavily annotated), scores, notes, and other documents relating to productions dating from the mid-1970s to circa 2021. In addition to these production files, there are smaller quantities of other material including: administrative files, correspondence, publicity, and reviews, journals of founding and original members Elizabeth LeCompte and Kate Valk, as well as material specifically documenting Ron Vawter's involvement with the group.

Special Projects, 1983-2023. X. Digital Files, circa 1985-2011.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: The Wooster Group is a contemporary experimental theater group based at 33 Wooster Street in New York City. Founded by Elizabeth LeCompte and Spalding Gray, the company has been active with an evolving membership since the mid-1970s and has created and performed over 50 works directed mostly by LeCompte. Founding members of the group include Kate Valk, Ron Vawter, Jim Clayburgh, Willem Dafoe, and Peyton Smith. The Wooster Group primarily presents performances from their permanent home, the Performing Garage, as well as touring internationally and performing at other venues in New York City. All Wooster Group productions are self-produced and highly collaborative. Collaborations have taken place with numerous artists from all media including Ken Kobland, Trisha Brown, John Lurie, David Linton, Bruce Odland, Jennifer Tipton, Hans Peter Kuhn, Eric Berryman, and Amir ElSaffar.
Note: The Wooster Group records (YCAL MSS 1560) includes material relating to most of the productions listed below, but is not comprehensive.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Collections are processed to a variety of levels, depending on the work necessary to make them usable, their perceived research value, the availability of staff, competing priorities, and whether or not further accruals are expected. The library attempts to provide a basic level of preservation and access for all collections, and does more extensive processing of higher priority collections as time and resources permit. These materials have been arranged and described according to national and local standards. For more information, please refer to the Beinecke Archival Description Unit Processing Manual.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Wooster Group records features material created, used by, and relating to the Wooster Group's productions, founders, and operations. The bulk of the collection consists of the production files, which includes scripts (many heavily annotated), scores, notes, and other documents relating to productions dating from the mid-1970s to circa 2021. In addition to these production files, there are smaller quantities of other material including: administrative files, correspondence, publicity, and reviews, journals of founding and original members Elizabeth LeCompte and Kate Valk, as well as material specifically documenting Ron Vawter's involvement with the group.

Material relating to Wooster Group productions varies somewhat from one production to the next, but tend to include scores, scripts, notes, research material, plans and schemas, various sorts of cues, cast and costume and prop lists, correspondence, drawings and blueprints, sheet music and lyrics, printed and promotional materials such as posters and programs, and box office and other financial records.
The Wooster Group administrative files in the collection include financial and legal records, calendars and schedules, and promotional materials.

Correspondence in the collection takes the form of general correspondence consisting of small files for individual and corporate correspondents, as well as larger files compiled by The Wooster Group for different kinds of queries received by the company. There are letters from domestic and foreign contributors to the theater, including established and aspiring actors and performers, playwrights, directors, and critics, as well as publishers and educational and cultural institutions.

Also included within the collection are writings, including essays by others, interviews, material relating to The Wooster Group Work Book, and miscellaneous other writings. The Essays subseries includes drafts and printed versions of work by others on The Wooster Group and theater generally. Essays on The Wooster Group offer critical reception of the company's work. The articles on some aspect of theater generally were likely collected by company members for research purposes.
Printed material in the collection consists of clippings, promotional ephemera relating to the Wooster Group, events at The Performing Garage by other companies, and performances by Spalding Gray.
Finally, the collection also includes born-digital material created by the Wooster Group. These include surtitle files, lighting cues, and an early video game titled Mind Mirror .
The collection is chiefly in English, with some materials in German, French, Dutch, Flemish, Spanish, Portugese, Italian, Danish, Swedish, Polish, Russian, and Hebrew.

userestrict.head: Conditions Governing Use
userestrict.p: The Wooster Group records is the physical property of the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. Literary rights, including copyright, belong to the authors or their legal heirs and assigns. For further information, consult the appropriate curator.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into four subseries: Theater, Theater Collaborations, Video and Film Productions, and Other Productions.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series I. includes material relating to productions and performances from throughout the Wooster Group's history and is subdivided for theater, theater collaborations, film and video, and other productions.

The Theater subseries contains material from 27 productions put on by The Wooster Group over a period of 45 years, from the Group's founding in the 1970s to 2020. Within the subseries, productions are arranged chronologically, beginning with Sakonnet Point (1975) and ending with The Mother (2020). Within each production, materials are arranged alphabetically by item and folder headings or material type. While the quantity and types of collection material can vary somewhat from one production to the next, productions tend to include scores, scripts, notes, research material, plans and schemas, various sorts of cues, cast and costume and prop lists, correspondence, drawings and blueprints, sheet music and lyrics, printed and promotional materials such as posters and programs, and box office and other financial records.

Materials provide evidence of textual and other sources used by the Group, adaptations to existing work and experimentation, preparations undertaken to stage performances, and the names and contributions of individuals associated with the company over time, as well as the odd controversy. The first three theater productions, for example, Sakonnet Point , Rumstick Road (1977), and Nayatt School (1978), which form the Rhode Island trilogy, along with Judith Point (1979), document Spalding Gray's involvement in the early years of the company and the group's use of media--audio recordings and fixed and moving images--in live performance.

Subsequent productions of Route 1 & 9 (The Last Act) (1981) and L.S.D. (1983) brought controversy. Materials for Route 1 & 9 include costume and prop lists, diagrams, notes, photographs, posters, scores and scripts, and time and video logs, but also documents relating to fallout stemming from backlash to the Group's adaptation of a Pigmeat Markham comedy routine in the middle parts of the performance. As a result of public and critical backlash, the Group lost a percentage of their 1981-1982 funding from the New York State Council on the Arts (NYSCA). The controversy is documented in a panel discussion including members of the company and an "Appeal of the Decision of the New York State Council on the Arts to Withhold Public Funds..." Correspondence relating to this controversy, including letters from members of the Group and NYSCA, as well as third party correspondents, can be found in Series III. Included are also letters denying The Wooster Group permission to use any or all of Our Town by Thornton Wilder.

The Wooster Group also ran into difficulty trying to secure rights to excerpts from The Crucible by Arthur Miller in their production of L.S.D. . L.S.D. production materials include a file with the heading "Jim Johnson's legal research on Arthur Miller's The Crucible " containing documents on copyright law and relevant case law for New York State. As with the Route 1 & 9 controversy, correspondence relating to this production, dating from 1982-1986, can be found in Series III. Included is a cease and desist letter from Miller's legal representatives. The Wooster Group's efforts to secure rights to Miller's play are also summarized in David Savran's Breaking the Rules: The Wooster Group (1988).

In later productions, material in Hamlet (2006) covers the Group's performance of Shakespeare's play, drawing on (and re-imagining) the Richard Burton production performed and broadcast in 1964. The materials in this file illustrate the process of adapting this particular production with scene breakdowns, transcripts from the original, annotated scripts, rehearsal and performance notes, and lighting setups and costume elements.

The material for La Didone (2007) documents the path the Wooster Group took to adapt the 17th century opera, utilizing imagery and visuals from the 1965 Mario Bava science fiction film Planet of the Vampires . This file includes transcripts of the film, notes, scripts, musical scores, libretti, lighting cues, as well as dramaturgical research materials.

The Vieux Carré (2009) production material documents the Wooster Group's adaptation of the Tennessee Williams play by the same name. This file includes a cease and desist letter concerning rehearsals of the production, along with technical notes, rehearsal and production notes, sheet music, and annotated scripts.

Other productions covered in the Theater subseries include: North Atlantic , Frank Dell's The Temptation of St. Antony , Brace Up! , The Emperor Jones , Fish Story , House/Lights , The Hairy Ape , To You, the Birdie (Phedre) , Poor Theater , Who's Your Dada? , Cry, Trojans , Early Shaker Spirituals , The Room , Town Hall Affair , The B-Side: "Negro Folklore from Texas State Prisons," A Record Album Interpretation , and A Pink Chair (In Place of a Fake Antique) .

It should be noted that scattered monographs can be found in the Theater subseries. The most common are printed versions of plays adapted by the Wooster Group. There are several copies, for example, most annotated, of Miller's The Crucible in L.S.D. . There are also a few books identified on prop lists and, finally, in a few additional cases, books appear to have been acquired for research purposes.

The Theater Collaborations subseries in Series I. consists of material from theater work undertaken with organizations and individuals outside the Wooster Group. The material outlines how collaboration with the Wooster Group was possible, including annotated scripts, production binder materials, and production materials created by collaborators.

The Video and Film subseries covers the approximate years 1986-2004. Included are drafts of screenplays as well as production scripts, research material, notes, production and distribution agreements and expenses, shot logs, publicity material, editor's logs, and correspondence related to several projects. Also included are screenplays and production materials for works identified as unproduced.

The Wooster Group came to employ the term "score" for a resource consisting of a source text or script with added staging, sound, lighting, or other information that might go into a performance. From the earliest productions in the 1970s, the company regularly used National brand analysis pads (notebooks) for this purpose. A source text or script, such as a clipped photocopy of a printed version of a text, would be pasted into the National analysis pad, and the marginal space outside the pasted text would allow for annotations. In some cases, items identified as "scores" consist only of script pages and no "scoring" annotations—strictly speaking, scripts. For some later theater productions, documents formatted with columns or blocks for "script," "stage direction," "video score," "sound score," and other relevant elements replaced the National brand notepads.

Some documents and files in Series I are either marked for or have been attributed to specific company members. Since many people have worked in the company over the years, when known or present, name attributions have been preserved in folder headings or notes. These are most common for scores, scripts, and other, usually mixed production "binders" and files. In addition, when present, post-it notes providing such attributions or other descriptive information, added by Wooster Group archivist Clay Hapaz, have been preserved at the back of the folders.

Additional information on individual Wooster Group productions may also be found among the journals, notebooks, and papers of founding and long-time company members Elizabeth LeCompte, Kate Valk, and Ron Vawter in Series VI through VIII respectively.
Critical discussion of productions and Wooster Group members can be found in writings and clippings in Series IV and V respectively.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series III. consists chiefly of correspondence relating to Wooster Group productions and business dating from the late 1970s onward. The series is subdivided for General correspondence consisting of small files for individual and corporate correspondents, arranged alphabetically, and Other correspondence, consisting chiefly of larger files compiled by The Wooster Group for different kinds of queries received by the company. There are letters from domestic and foreign contributors to the theater, including established and aspiring actors and performers, playwrights, directors, and critics, as well as publishers and educational and cultural institutions. Correspondents include Romulus Linney, Meredith Monk, and Carolee Schneemann, among others. In addition to original incoming correspondence, printouts of email received by the company and photocopies of incoming and outgoing letters can also be found.

Wooster Group members represented in the correspondence files include: Elizabeth LeCompte, Spalding Gray, Kate Valk, Willem Dafoe, Ron Vawter, Peyton Smith, Jim Clayburgh, Paul Berman (Administrator), Linda Chapman (General Manager), Cynthia Hedstrom (Producing Director), Tracy Leipold, Marianne Weems (Assistant Director), Andrea Most (Administrative Director), Anne Reis, Kim Whitener (Managing Director), Richard Kimmel, Joel Bassin (Managing Director), and others.
In addition to Wooster Group business, there are letters to LeCompte and Spalding Gray, dating from the early 1970s, from Performance Group founders Richard Schechner and Joan Macintosh.

The bulk of the Other correspondence consists of inquiries (and responses) relating to the following: one, internships and jobs with The Wooster Group; two, interviews with company members; three, participation by company members at events; four, opportunities to observe company rehearsals; five, use of photographs and video; and six, Willem Dafoe. There are also files for correspondence and other materials relating to controversies around productions of Route 1 & 9 (The Last Act) (1981) and L.S.D. (1983).

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into four subseries: Essays by Others, Interviews, The Wooster Group Work Book , and Other Writings.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series IV. Writings is subdivided for essays by others, interviews, material relating to The Wooster Group Work Book , and miscellaneous other writings.

The Essays subseries includes drafts and printed versions of work by others on The Wooster Group and theater generally. Essays on The Wooster Group offer critical reception of the company's work. The articles on some aspect of theater generally were likely collected by company members for research purposes.

There are both drafts and printed versions of interviews conducted with Elizabeth LeCompte, Kate Valk, and other members of the company. Interviews span a period of almost 40 years, from an early 1981 discussion between Italian academic Maddalena Raimondi Capasso and LeCompte on the latter's emerging practice to a 2019 discussion between playwright Sara Farrington, a former Wooster Group intern, and theater veteran Kate Valk.
In addition to the essays and interviews, there are various documents, as well as a draft and proofs, of The Wooster Group Work Book (Routledge, 2007) by Andrew Quick.

Other Writings includes a draft of David Savran's 1985 thesis, "Alternate Routes: The Wooster Group 1975-85," and possibly the revised Breaking the Rules: The Wooster Group (Theatre Communications Group, 1988).

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into two subseries: Press Clippings and Other Material.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series V. Printed Materials is subdivided for press clippings and other material.

The subseries for press clippings is subdivided for content relating to productions by The Wooster Group, founding members of the company, and other topics. The Productions subdivision features publicity for and reviews of productions dating from Rumstick Road (1977) to Early Shaker Spirituals (2014). Generally, the reviews document how Wooster Group productions were covered in the press over the first two decades of the company. There are multiple reviews in most files, with reviews by different critics for different publications. One can also trace the work of individual critics over time. Critics whose work appears in New York and other area papers and magazines covering cultural events during this period include Mel Gussow, Michael Feingold, Marilyn Stasio, Tish Dace, James Leverett, David Sterritt, Erika Munk, Don Shewey, David Savran, and Stephen Holden, among others.

While materials consist chiefly of clippings and photocopies of clippings from domestic and foreign newspapers and magazines, there are several larger files for touring productions consolidating clippings from different publications and a few mixed files for foreign productions containing correspondence and other material, such as press kits.

The subdivision for People includes files for prominent early members of The Wooster Group, including Elizabeth LeCompte, Spalding Gray, Willem Dafoe, Ron Vawter, and Kate Valk. The final subdivision brings together other files not identified by production or company member. There are files on theater, fundraising, and film, as well as for the "Glascow press," "Press originals," "Toronto press," and "Wooster Group originals."

The bulk of the material in the clippings subseries is in English, German, and French. Smaller quantities of material and/or single items can also be found in Dutch, Flemish, Spanish, Portugese, Italian, Danish, Swedish, Polish, Russian, and Hebrew.
Other materials include promotional ephemera relating to the Wooster Group, events at The Performing Garage by other companies, and performances by Spalding Gray.

arrangement.p: Organized into two subseries: Journals and Notebooks.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Elizabeth LeCompte Journals and Notebooks series is subdivided by format for hardcover volumes (journals) and spiral-bound notebooks and arranged chronologically within each subdivision. Except for a childhood diary dating from 1956, the journals date from the mid-1970s to circa 2008 and the notebooks from the early 1970s to circa 2019. Contents feature contact information, to-do lists, calendars and scheduling information, financial data, bibliographic notes, personal entries, rehearsal and performance notes, and drawings and diagrams. The journals and notebooks document LeCompte's commitment to The Wooster Group over a period of almost five decades and include references to fellow company members and productions dating from Sakonnet Point in the mid-1970s to Nayatt School Redux in 2018.

Various materials can also be found pasted, taped, or laid in to the journals and notebooks. These materials include photographs, postcards and other printed ephemera, letters, documents, and even paint samples. There are photographs of LeCompte, Spalding Gray, Willem Dafoe, Jack Dafoe, and others. Folded items found laid in have been unfolded and, in some cases, removed and housed separately either after the originating volume or notebook or in oversize.
